name: Jury Selection and Public Data
title: Jury Selection and Public Data
answer: This page covers how public records and data about potential jurors, jury pools, and past verdicts are used to inform jury selection in civil and criminal litigation. It includes voter registration, property records, social media profiles, court dockets, and demographic data that lawyers and consultants assemble before voir dire. The focus is on prediction and analytics rather than on the legal rules of challenges for cause or peremptory strikes. It also distinguishes between publicly available information and data that is restricted or obtained through discovery.

crumbs.name: Knowledge Based Professions and their Future

sections.body: This page covers how public records and data about potential jurors, jury pools, and past verdicts are used to inform jury selection in civil and criminal litigation. It includes voter registration, property records, social media profiles, court dockets, and demographic data that lawyers and consultants assemble before voir dire. The focus is on prediction and analytics rather than on the legal rules of challenges for cause or peremptory strikes. It also distinguishes between publicly available information and data that is restricted or obtained through discovery.
sections.heading: Scope

sections.body: The work runs on ordinary data infrastructure: cleaned extracts from county voter files, property assessor rolls, state court dockets, and commercial data brokers, joined to a case's jury pool list. Social media profiles and public posts are often collected through licensed data providers or manual review. The resulting tables are stored in case management or analytics software, and scoring models are run on standard business hardware or cloud services.
sections.heading: What it runs on

sections.body: Analysts build a profile of favorable and unfavorable jurors from past verdicts, voir dire answers, and demographic patterns in the venue. Each potential juror is scored on factors such as age, occupation, home ownership, civic participation, and public posts that suggest attitudes toward the parties or issues. The scores are often produced by weighted checklists or simple regression models rather than deep learning, and they are updated as voir dire reveals new information. The output is a ranking or color-coded list that the trial team uses during jury selection.
sections.heading: How the work is done

sections.body: Using public data in jury selection raises serious questions about juror privacy, accuracy, and discrimination. Voter and property files may be outdated or contain errors, and social media profiles can be misattributed or taken out of context. Courts and ethics rules restrict some forms of juror investigation, and peremptory strikes based on race, gender, or other protected classes remain unlawful. Lawyers must document the provenance of each data point and be ready to explain that a strike was based on permissible, case-specific reasons rather than a protected characteristic.
sections.heading: Rights, risk and provenance

sections.body: Jury selection tools are moving toward real-time analysis of public posts and faster matching of juror lists against commercial and government databases. Some vendors are adding natural language processing to summarize social media histories and flag risk topics before voir dire. At the same time, courts and legislatures are paying closer attention to juror privacy, and rules may narrow what public data can be collected or how it can be used. The likely result is a more automated but more closely regulated practice, with greater emphasis on audit trails and explainable scores.
